Common e-commerce SEO mistakes and how to assess them

Online stores can create many more URLs than useful search destinations. Effective e-commerce SEO is partly the work of deciding which pages should exist for customers and which variations should not compete for indexing.

By Shahir Salehi3 minute readPractical guide

In this guide

  1. Letting every filter become a search page
  2. Treating categories as empty containers
  3. Ignoring variant URL behavior
  4. Removing products without a decision
  5. Publishing structured data that disagrees with the page
  6. Overlooking the buying journey
  7. Changing too much without verification

Letting every filter become a search page

Filters help shoppers, but combinations of color, size, sort order, and stock status can create large numbers of similar URLs. Some combinations may serve distinct demand; many will not. Review actual usefulness, available products, internal links, and platform behavior before deciding which variations deserve stable, indexable destinations. A blanket rule can remove valuable pages or leave unnecessary duplication.

Treating categories as empty containers

A category page should help people choose a useful direction. Clear names, sensible grouping, concise supporting information, and relevant products all matter. Long generic paragraphs added solely for keywords can obscure the shopping task. Check the navigation and product discovery experience as well as the metadata. The category structure should reflect how customers understand the catalogue.

Ignoring variant URL behavior

Product variants may use separate URLs or change state on one page. Canonical tags, availability, selected options, and internal links need to agree with the chosen approach. A customer arriving at a specific variant should see the expected information. Test direct visits rather than assuming that a selector working from the main product page proves every URL works.

Removing products without a decision

A discontinued item may have links, search interest, and customers looking for support or a replacement. Decide whether to retain useful information, point to a genuinely equivalent item, or return an appropriate error. Redirecting every removed product to a broad category can be confusing. Temporary unavailability needs a different policy from permanent removal.

Publishing structured data that disagrees with the page

Product markup must reflect visible, accurate information such as price, availability, and genuine review data where supplied. Do not invent ratings or assume that adding schema guarantees a rich result. Check representative templates after updates, especially when currency, stock, or variant logic changes. Validation of syntax is only the first check; factual agreement matters too.

Overlooking the buying journey

A technically accessible product still needs useful descriptions, dimensions or specifications, delivery information, and clear terms. Marketing cannot compensate indefinitely for missing stock or confusing checkout. Review mobile behavior and actual orders alongside search data. A rise in organic sessions may be less valuable than a smaller number of visits to products the business can fulfill profitably.

Changing too much without verification

Catalogue and template changes can affect many pages at once. Capture a baseline, test representative categories and variants, and release with a rollback or recovery plan appropriate to the platform. Recheck redirects, canonicals, internal links, feeds, and purchase tracking. Prioritize corrections by business relevance rather than the number of warnings a crawler produces.

Put it into practice

  • Choose indexable filter destinations deliberately.
  • Make categories useful to shoppers.
  • Verify direct variant URLs and canonical behavior.
  • Define a lifecycle policy for unavailable products.
  • Check live data and purchase journeys after template changes.
